title: Moonrise, Hernandez, 1941 — one shot, no light meter, and seconds to spare
sources: Wikipedia: Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico — taken by Ansel Adams late in the afternoon on 1 November 1941 from the shoulder of US 84/285 at Hernandez, New Mexico; in October 1941 Interior Secretary Harold Ickes had hired Adams for six months to photograph lands under the Department of the Interior; travelling through the Chama River valley toward Española, the party saw a church and cemetery and pulled to the side of the road; they scrambled to set up the tripod and camera with only moments of light left; Adams: 'I could not find my Weston exposure meter!'; he realised he knew the luminance of the moon, 250 candles per square foot, and worked out the exposure; he captured a single image with the sunset lighting the white crosses; reversing the film holder for a duplicate, the sunlight passed from the crosses — 'I was a few seconds too late!'; Adams personally made over 1,300 prints of it; a 1948 print sold for $609,600 at Sotheby's in 2006, and a mural-sized print for $930,000 at Christie's in 2021

Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1914 the first contingent of the Australian Imperial Force departs Albany; 1993 the Maastricht Treaty takes effect, formally establishing the European Union

Photos (public domain): Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico; Ansel Adams's personnel file photograph; Adams's 1941–42 photographs for the Department of the Interior (Taos Pueblo, Old Faithful, Castle Geyser, Boulder Dam, Grand Canyon, Glacier, a leaf) — National Archives
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): the moon rising, a desert highway

post.facebook:
On this day in 1941, Ansel Adams made one of the most famous photographs in history — in a single shot, with no light meter.

The government had hired him to photograph America's national lands. Driving through New Mexico late in the afternoon, he saw it: a village, a church, white crosses, and the moon rising over the mountains. He pulled off the road at Hernandez and scrambled to set up his camera.

Then he couldn't find his exposure meter. "The situation was desperate," he wrote — the sun was slipping behind the clouds. Then he remembered he knew how bright the moon was: 250 candles per square foot. He worked out the exposure and took one picture. When he flipped the film holder for a second, the sunlight had left the crosses. "I was a few seconds too late!"

That lone negative became Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico. Adams printed it more than 1,300 times himself, and in 2021 a mural-sized print sold for $930,000.

Also on 1 November: Australia's first troops sailed for the Great War (1914), and the Maastricht Treaty created the EU (1993).

youtube.description:
1 November 1941: driving through New Mexico, Ansel Adams saw the moon rising over the village of Hernandez, its church and white crosses lit by the last sun. He couldn't find his light meter — so he worked out the exposure from the brightness of the moon, 250 candles per square foot, and took a single picture. His second shot was a few seconds too late. That lone negative became Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico; Adams printed it more than 1,300 times, and a print sold for $930,000 in 2021.

Also on 1 November: Australia's first troops sail for WW1 (1914) and the Maastricht Treaty (1993).
